questions.title: What standard of review applies to TTAB likelihood of confusion determinations?
questions.question_body: I'm reading this Federal Circuit opinion and trying to understand the standard of review. The court says it reviews legal conclusions de novo but findings of fact for substantial evidence. But then it says "likelihood of confusion is a question of law, based on findings of relevant underlying facts, namely findings under the DuPont factors." And each DuPont factor is a question of fact tested for substantial evidence. So is likelihood of confusion ultimately a question of law or fact? And what does "substantial evidence" actually mean in practice?

questions.title: What does "legally identical" mean when the services aren't actually identical?
questions.question_body: The Board found that credit card services and banking/financing services are "legally identical, in part." But CC Serve offers credit card services while Apex offers banking services—they're not the same thing. How can services be "legally identical" when they're different? What is the legal significance of this designation versus just saying they're "similar" or "related"? Does "legally identical" create a presumption of confusion?

questions.title: Why does evidence of third-party similar marks weaken a trademark's protection?
questions.question_body: The court discusses how third-party uses of similar marks can show that a mark is "relatively weak and entitled to only a narrow scope of protection." The theory is that when a field is crowded with similar marks, "customers will be more adept at distinguishing marks from each other and are less likely to be confused." I don't understand this reasoning—if anything, wouldn't more similar marks in the marketplace cause MORE confusion, not less? Why does a "crowded field" mean the mark gets weaker protection?

questions.title: Why must the Board use consistent definitions of "similarity" across different DuPont factors?
questions.question_body: The Federal Circuit held that the Board erred by using a narrow definition of "similar services" in the sixth DuPont factor analysis (limiting it to credit card services only) after finding the services were "highly similar" in the second factor. But aren't these different factors asking different questions? The second factor asks about similarity of the parties' goods to each other, while the sixth asks about third-party marks on similar goods. Why must the Board use the same scope of "similarity" for both factors? Couldn't there be a legitimate reason to define the relevant market differently for each factor?

questions.title: Why was the first DuPont factor analysis vacated when the error was with the sixth factor?
questions.question_body: The court vacated the Board's analysis of the first DuPont factor (similarity of the marks themselves in appearance, sound, connotation, and commercial impression) even though the legal error was with the sixth factor (third-party uses). The court says this is because "reconsideration of the sixth DuPont factor may result in a different determination of the mark's commercial strength or weakness and affect the overall commercial impression." But the first factor is about comparing the two marks' appearance, sound, and meaning—what does that have to do with third-party uses? How does the strength of a mark affect the first factor analysis?

questions.title: How many third-party uses are needed to establish that a mark is weak under the sixth DuPont factor?
questions.question_body: The Board found that nine third-party Aspire-formative marks for credit card services weren't enough to show the mark is weak, citing cases that found 14 marks (Jack Wolfskin) and 26 marks (Juice Generation) to be sufficient. Is there an established threshold number? Does the number vary by industry or type of goods? The opinion says nine doesn't rise to the level of "considerable" or "ubiquitous"—but how should a practitioner know whether their evidence of third-party uses will be enough?

questions.title: Why were costs awarded to the appellant when they lost on one of three factors?
questions.question_body: The court awarded costs to Apex as the appellant, even though the Board's opposition decision was affirmed in part (the second factor finding was affirmed). Apex won on two factors (vacatur and remand) but lost on one (the second factor was affirmed). I thought costs typically go to the prevailing party. Who is considered the "prevailing party" in a partially affirmed, partially vacated appeal like this? Does getting a vacatur and remand count as "prevailing" for costs purposes even though the underlying opposition was sustained?
